title: Set Team and Individual Performance Goals to Enhancing Team Performance

lessons.title: Setting clear goals
lessons.html:
Setting clear goals

Teams perform best when everyone knows what is expected, why it matters and how they are doing. This practical module covers setting team and individual goals and using them to improve performance in the orchard or vineyard.

Linking goals to the farm's targets

Start with the farm's targets for the season: yield, packout, cost per hectare, quality, safety. Break them down into goals for operations and teams. For example, a packout target leads to goals for thinning accuracy and careful picking; a cost target leads to goals for productivity and reduced waste.

SMART goals

LetterMeaningExample
SSpecificThin block 5 Golden Delicious to the spacing standard
MMeasurableAt least 9 out of 10 sample trees within the fruit count range
AAchievableBased on team size and known work rates
RRelevantSupports fruit size and packout
TTime-boundFinished by Friday

Team and individual goals

Team goals build cooperation: 'Team A finishes block 5 by Friday with no quality failures.' Individual goals help each worker grow: 'Thandi improves pruning speed to the standard rate while keeping quality,' or 'Johan completes sprayer operator training this month.' Agree individual goals with the worker rather than imposing them; people commit more to goals they helped set.

Include quality and safety

Goals that measure only speed lead to poor work and injuries. Always pair output goals with quality and safety goals, such as damage percentage at picking, correct PPE use and zero lost-time injuries.

Communicating goals

Explain goals at the morning briefing in plain language. Display team goals and progress on a board at the shed. Make sure team leaders understand and repeat them.

lessons.title: Monitoring performance and giving feedback
lessons.html:
Monitoring performance and giving feedback

Measuring progress

Use the measures in your goals: output per worker or team, quality sample results, attendance, safety incidents. Collect them daily from job cards, quality checks and team leaders. Share results with teams regularly so they know where they stand.

Quality sampling

Check a fixed number of trees, vines or bins per worker or team each day. Use a simple score sheet. Be consistent - the same standard for everyone, every day.

Feedback that works

  • Timely: give feedback while the work is fresh, ideally in the row.
  • Specific: 'These three spurs were cut too short' is better than 'bad pruning'.
  • Balanced: say what is going well and what needs to change.
  • Private for correction, public for praise.
  • Two-way: ask the worker what is making the task difficult.

Coaching

When a worker is below standard, coach: demonstrate again, let them try, and watch until they get it right. Pair them with a strong worker for a day. Check again the next day. Most performance problems are solved by clear standards, good tools and coaching.

Recognising good performance

Recognise teams and individuals who reach or exceed goals: mention them at the briefing, display results, and use the farm's incentive or award schemes fairly. Recognition must be based on the agreed measures so that it is seen as fair.

Performance discussions

At the end of a season or period, hold short individual discussions: review goals, results, strengths and areas to develop, and agree new goals and training needs. Record the outcome and share it with HR as the farm's process requires.

lessons.title: Building a high-performing team
lessons.html:
Building a high-performing team

What makes a team perform

  • A clear common goal everyone understands.
  • Clear roles: who does what, who leads.
  • Skills: everyone trained for their tasks.
  • Resources: tools, PPE, transport, materials on time.
  • Trust and respect among members and with the foreman.
  • Fair treatment and fair rewards.

Removing barriers

Often teams underperform because of obstacles they cannot fix themselves: blunt secateurs, late transport, bins not delivered, unclear instructions, conflict between members. Ask the team what slows them down and fix what you can. This shows that you take their performance seriously.

Team leaders

Develop strong team leaders. Give them responsibility for daily goals, quality checks and first-line problem solving. Meet them each day, coach them and back their decisions in front of the team.

Handling underperformance

If an individual repeatedly misses goals after coaching and support, follow the farm's performance management process with HR. Distinguish between inability (needs training or a different role) and unwillingness (may be a disciplinary matter). Keep records of goals, feedback and support given.

Team problem solving

Involve the team in solving recurring problems. For example, if picking damage is too high, hold a short meeting: show damaged fruit, ask the team what causes it, and agree changes such as emptying bags more gently or not overfilling bins. Then measure again.

Diversity and inclusion

Teams include men and women, young and old, local and migrant workers. Make sure goals and recognition are fair for all, that nobody is excluded, and that harassment or discrimination is not tolerated.

Key points

  • Link team and individual goals to farm targets.
  • Use SMART goals that include quality and safety, not only speed.
  • Measure consistently and give timely, specific feedback.
  • Coach workers below standard before formal steps.
  • Remove barriers and involve the team in solving problems.
